title: Token Budget Calculator
problemMarkdown:
## Problem

Implement `ContextBudget` so an orchestrator can decide how much retrieved context it may include.

Given a total context window, a reserve for the response, a system prompt size and a maximum history allowance, calculate how many tokens remain for retrieval, and how many chunks of a given size will fit.

## Requirements

- `AvailableForRetrieval` returns the remaining tokens after the reserve, system prompt and history allowance.
- `MaxChunks(int tokensPerChunk)` returns how many whole chunks fit, never negative.
- `EstimateCostUsd` accounts for input and output being priced differently.
- Guard against a configuration where the fixed allocations exceed the window — return zero rather than a negative number.

## Why this matters

"It usually fits" fails the day a user pastes a thirty-page document into the chat. Context is a budgeted resource.

tests.name: Available retrieval budget subtracts all fixed allocations
tests.hint: Subtract the response reserve, system prompt and history allowance from the total window.

tests.name: Budget never returns a negative value
tests.hint: Clamp the result at zero — a misconfiguration should not produce a negative budget.

tests.name: MaxChunks guards against a non-positive chunk size
tests.hint: Return 0 when tokensPerChunk is zero or negative rather than dividing by zero.

tests.name: Cost calculation prices input and output separately
tests.hint: Output tokens usually cost several times input tokens, so they cannot share a rate.

tests.name: No unimplemented members remain
tests.hint: Replace every TODO with a real implementation.

explanation: Two details matter beyond the arithmetic. Clamping at zero means a misconfiguration degrades to "no retrieval" rather than producing a negative number that propagates silently into chunk counts. And pricing input and output separately reflects reality: output typically costs three to five times input, so a single blended rate will understate the cost of a verbose feature. Using `decimal` rather than `double` avoids the floating-point drift that shows up when these figures are aggregated across millions of requests for chargeback.

title: Resilient LLM Client with Correct Retry Policy
problemMarkdown:
## Problem

Implement `ShouldRetry` and `GetDelay` for an LLM HTTP client.

## Requirements

- Retry on 429 and on 5xx responses.
- Never retry 4xx other than 429 — the request itself is wrong and retrying costs the same and fails the same.
- Honour a `Retry-After` header when present.
- Otherwise use exponential backoff **with jitter**.
- Stop after `maxAttempts`.

## Why this matters

Without jitter, every client retries at the same moment and recreates the spike that caused the throttling. Retrying a 400 three times is three charges for the same malformed request.

tests.name: Retries on 429
tests.hint: HttpStatusCode.TooManyRequests is 429 and is the canonical retryable response.

tests.name: Retries on 5xx
tests.hint: Treat any status code of 500 or above as transient.

tests.name: Does not retry other 4xx responses
tests.hint: A 400 or 401 will fail identically on every attempt — do not retry them.

tests.name: Honours the Retry-After header
tests.hint: response.Headers.RetryAfter carries the server's own guidance; prefer it over your own backoff.

tests.name: Applies jitter to the backoff
tests.hint: Without jitter every client retries in lockstep and recreates the spike.

tests.name: No unimplemented members remain
tests.hint: Replace every TODO with a real implementation.

explanation: The retry set is the part people get wrong in both directions: retrying everything wastes money on requests that cannot succeed, while retrying nothing turns a transient throttle into a user-visible failure. `Retry-After` takes precedence because the server knows when capacity returns and your backoff is a guess. Jitter is not a refinement — it is the difference between a throttled fleet recovering and a throttled fleet synchronising into a thundering herd that keeps the service down.

title: Server-Sent Events Streaming Endpoint
problemMarkdown:
## Problem

Implement an ASP.NET Core endpoint that streams an LLM response to the browser over server-sent events.

## Requirements

- Set the SSE content type and disable buffering.
- Flush after every chunk.
- Propagate `HttpContext.RequestAborted` into the provider call so closing the tab stops generation.
- Handle failure mid-stream by emitting an error **event** — you cannot send an error status after a 200.
- Accumulate the content server-side and persist it, including when cancelled.

## Why this matters

Without cancellation you keep paying for tokens nobody will read. Without the error event, a mid-stream failure leaves the user staring at a half-finished sentence.

tests.name: Sets the server-sent events content type
tests.hint: Response.Headers.ContentType must be text/event-stream.

tests.name: Disables proxy buffering
tests.hint: Without this header a reverse proxy may buffer the whole response and defeat streaming.

tests.name: Flushes after each chunk
tests.hint: Nothing reaches the browser until the response body is flushed.

tests.name: Propagates cancellation into the provider call
tests.hint: Pass HttpContext.RequestAborted down so generation stops when the client disconnects.

tests.name: Emits an error event rather than a status code
tests.hint: After a 200 the status is already sent; the error must travel as an SSE event.

tests.name: Persists accumulated content in a finally block
tests.hint: Partial content is usually still worth keeping, including on cancellation.

explanation: Three details separate a working implementation from a demo. Disabling proxy buffering: without it, a reverse proxy holds the whole response and the user waits exactly as long as they would have without streaming. Cancellation: `RequestAborted` is what stops you paying for a response nobody will read, and on a busy system that is a measurable share of the bill. And the error event: once a 200 is on the wire you cannot change the status, so the protocol itself needs a failure channel — and the `finally` block uses `CancellationToken.None` deliberately, because the persistence must complete even though the request token is already cancelled.

title: Structure-Aware Chunker with Overlap
problemMarkdown:
## Problem

Implement a chunker that respects document structure.

## Requirements

- Prepend the heading path to every chunk so a mid-document chunk remains identifiable.
- Accumulate paragraphs up to a target token count.
- Carry an overlap of the tail into the next chunk so a boundary-spanning answer stays retrievable.
- Emit tables whole, with their headers — never through the text splitter.
- Never exceed the maximum token ceiling.

## Why this matters

A table split from its headers produces chunks that retrieve confidently and answer wrongly, which is worse than not retrieving at all.

tests.name: Prepends the heading path to each chunk
tests.hint: Join the heading path and prefix it to the chunk text — the cheapest large retrieval win available.

tests.name: Emits tables whole rather than splitting them
tests.hint: Check for a table section and yield it intact with its headers.

tests.name: Accumulates to a target token count
tests.hint: Buffer paragraphs until the target is reached, then emit.

tests.name: Carries overlap into the following chunk
tests.hint: Take the tail of the emitted chunk and seed the next buffer with it.

tests.name: Uses the token counter rather than character length
tests.hint: Budgets are in tokens; character counts diverge badly for code and non-English text.

tests.name: No unimplemented members remain
tests.hint: Replace the TODO with a real implementation.

explanation: The heading prefix is the highest-value line in this implementation: a chunk beginning "Handbook > Leave > Parental Leave" embeds far more usefully than one starting mid-sentence, and it costs a handful of tokens. Overlap exists for the case where the answer sits across a boundary — without it, neither adjacent chunk contains a complete answer and retrieval looks broken for no visible reason. Counting tokens rather than characters matters because the divergence is large for code and for non-English text, where a character-based budget silently produces chunks two or three times the intended size.

title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion
problemMarkdown:
## Problem

Implement reciprocal rank fusion to combine keyword and vector search results.

## Requirements

- Score each document as the sum of `weight / (k + rank)` across both lists, with `k = 60`.
- Use **rank position**, never the raw score — BM25 and cosine values are not comparable.
- Documents appearing in both lists accumulate both contributions.
- Return results ordered by fused score, limited to `topK`.

## Why this matters

Normalising incomparable scores requires calibration that breaks whenever the corpus or model changes. Ranks need none.

tests.name: Uses the standard smoothing constant
tests.hint: k = 60 is the conventional value and limits how much the top positions dominate.

tests.name: Scores from rank position rather than raw score
tests.hint: Use the loop index as the rank; ignore the incoming relevance scores entirely.

tests.name: Accumulates contributions from both lists
tests.hint: A document present in both lists must have both contributions summed.

tests.name: Applies the configured weights
tests.hint: Weighting lets you tune toward keyword for identifier-heavy corpora.

tests.name: Orders by fused score and limits results
tests.hint: Sort descending by the accumulated score, then take topK.

tests.name: No unimplemented members remain
tests.hint: Replace the TODO with a real implementation.

explanation: The whole point of RRF is that it needs no calibration. BM25 scores are unbounded and depend on corpus statistics; cosine similarities are bounded and cluster in a narrow band. Any attempt to normalise them into a common scale has to be re-tuned whenever the corpus grows or the embedding model changes. Ranks sidestep that entirely. The `k = 60` constant flattens the curve so that being ranked first rather than third in one list does not overwhelm a document that ranked well in both — which is exactly the behaviour you want when each retrieval leg has a different blind spot.

title: Schema-Constrained Extraction with Bounded Retry
problemMarkdown:
## Problem

Implement an extraction method that produces a validated typed record or routes to human review.

## Requirements

- Request structured output using a JSON schema.
- Use temperature 0 — extraction is not a creative task.
- Validate business rules after parsing: schema compliance is not correctness.
- On failure, retry **once** with the specific error fed back to the model.
- After the second failure, return null so the caller can route to human review. Never loop.

## Why this matters

A date can be well-formed and absurd. A total can be positive and fail to reconcile. The schema guarantees shape, not sense.

tests.name: Requests structured output via a schema
tests.hint: Attach a JSON schema so generation is constrained during decoding rather than merely requested.

tests.name: Uses temperature zero
tests.hint: Extraction is deterministic work; sampling variation only introduces errors.

tests.name: Validates business rules beyond the schema
tests.hint: Check that dates are plausible and totals are positive — the schema cannot.

tests.name: Retries at most once with the error fed back
tests.hint: A bounded loop of two attempts, appending the specific failure to the conversation.

tests.name: Returns null rather than guessing
tests.hint: Human review is the correct destination for an extraction that cannot be validated.

tests.name: No unimplemented members remain
tests.hint: Replace the TODO with a real implementation.

explanation: The bounded retry is the design decision worth noticing. One corrective attempt with the specific error is genuinely useful — models correct well when told exactly what was wrong. A second corrective attempt rarely helps and an unbounded loop turns a bad document into an unbounded bill. Returning null is not a failure of the implementation; it is the implementation working, because an invoice that cannot be validated belongs with a human rather than in the ledger. Note also that the retry appends the model's own failed output to the conversation, which gives it the context to see what it produced rather than starting blind.

title: Bounded Agent Loop with Repetition Detection
problemMarkdown:
## Problem

Implement the core agent loop with all four mandatory bounds.

## Requirements

- Stop after `maxSteps`.
- Accumulate cost and stop when the ceiling is exceeded — checked after **every** inference.
- Apply a wall-clock timeout via a linked cancellation token.
- Detect a repeated tool call with identical arguments and tell the model explicitly to try something else.
- Return the partial result rather than throwing when a bound is hit.

## Why this matters

An unbounded agent loop is an unbounded invoice. Repetition detection breaks more loops than raising the step limit ever will.

tests.name: Bounds the number of steps
tests.hint: A for loop to request.MaxSteps, not an open-ended while.

tests.name: Checks the cost ceiling after every inference
tests.hint: Accumulate usage cost and compare inside the loop, not after it.

tests.name: Applies a wall-clock timeout
tests.hint: Link the caller's token with a timeout so a slow tool cannot hold the run open.

tests.name: Detects repeated tool calls
tests.hint: Hash the tool name plus arguments and check membership before executing.

tests.name: Tells the model when it is repeating
tests.hint: Return a message saying the call was already made and it should try a different approach.

tests.name: Returns a partial result instead of throwing
tests.hint: Hitting a bound is an expected outcome, not an exception.

explanation: Repetition detection is the control that does the most work in practice. An agent that loops is not usually stuck because the step limit is too low — it is stuck because nothing told it that repeating the same call will produce the same result. Feeding that back explicitly gives the model the information it needs to change approach. Checking cost inside the loop rather than after it is the second important detail: the point of a ceiling is to stop spending, and a check that runs after the run completes has already spent the money.

title: Hybrid Search Query with pgvector
problemMarkdown:
## Problem

Write a PostgreSQL query that performs hybrid retrieval with permission filtering.

## Requirements

- A vector leg using the cosine distance operator with an ORDER BY and LIMIT.
- A keyword leg using full-text search.
- Fuse the two with reciprocal rank fusion.
- Apply the permission filter **inside both legs**, not afterwards.
- Return the top 20 fused results.

## Why this matters

Filtering after retrieval means restricted content was already loaded into memory and possibly logged. The filter belongs in the query.
starterCode:
-- Parameters: $1 = query embedding, $2 = user's group array, $3 = query text

WITH vector_hits AS (
    -- TODO: nearest neighbours with the permission filter applied here
),
keyword_hits AS (
    -- TODO: full-text matches with the permission filter applied here
)
-- TODO: fuse on rank and return the top 20

tests.name: Uses the cosine distance operator
tests.hint: pgvector's <=> operator is cosine distance and is what the HNSW index supports.

tests.name: Applies the permission filter in the vector leg
tests.hint: The array overlap operator && checks whether the user's groups intersect the chunk's ACL.

tests.name: Includes a keyword leg
tests.hint: Full-text search covers the exact identifiers that vectors miss.

tests.name: Ranks rather than combining raw scores
tests.hint: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY ...) gives the rank position for fusion.

tests.name: Fuses with the reciprocal rank formula
tests.hint: 1.0 / (60 + rank), summed across both legs.

tests.name: Limits the final result set
tests.hint: Return the top 20 fused results.

solutionCode:
-- $1 = query embedding, $2 = user's group array, $3 = query text

WITH vector_hits AS (
    SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY embedding <=> $1) AS rank
    FROM document_chunks
    -- Permission filter INSIDE the leg: restricted rows are never read.
    WHERE allowed_groups && $2::text[]
    ORDER BY embedding <=> $1
    LIMIT 50
),
keyword_hits AS (
    SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
        ORDER BY ts_rank(content_tsv, plainto_tsquery('english', $3)) DESC) AS rank
    FROM document_chunks
    WHERE content_tsv @@ plainto_tsquery('english', $3)
      AND allowed_groups && $2::text[]
    LIMIT 50
)
SELECT c.id,
       c.content,
       c.page_number,
       COALESCE(1.0 / (60 + v.rank), 0) + COALESCE(1.0 / (60 + k.rank), 0) AS fused_score
FROM document_chunks c
LEFT JOIN vector_hits  v ON v.id = c.id
LEFT JOIN keyword_hits k ON k.id = c.id
WHERE v.id IS NOT NULL OR k.id IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY fused_score DESC
LIMIT 20;
explanation: The filter placement is the security point: applying `allowed_groups && $2` inside each CTE means the database never returns rows the user cannot see, so restricted content never enters your process, your logs or your telemetry. A `WHERE` clause on the outer query would be functionally similar here but is a habit that breaks the moment someone adds a `LIMIT` before it. The `COALESCE` handles documents that appear in only one leg — they still score, which is exactly what you want when one retrieval method has a blind spot the other covers. Each leg retrieves 50 candidates so the fusion has material to work with before the final 20 are taken.

title: Streaming Chat Component with Cancellation
problemMarkdown:
## Problem

Implement an Angular service that consumes a server-sent events stream and exposes it as an observable.

## Requirements

- Open an `EventSource`-style connection and emit each token as it arrives.
- Handle the `error` event type from the server as a stream error, not a silent stop.
- Close the connection when the subscriber unsubscribes so the server sees the disconnect.
- Accumulate the text so the component can render progressively.

## Why this matters

If the browser does not close the connection on unsubscribe, the server keeps generating and you keep paying.

tests.name: Returns an Observable
tests.hint: Wrap the connection in an Observable so subscribers control its lifetime.

tests.name: Handles the token event
tests.hint: Listen for the named 'token' event and emit its text.

tests.name: Treats the server error event as a stream error
tests.hint: Call observer.error so the component can show a failure state.

tests.name: Closes the connection on teardown
tests.hint: The Observable teardown function must close the connection, or the server keeps generating.

tests.name: Completes on the done event
tests.hint: The server's 'done' event should complete the Observable.

tests.name: No unimplemented members remain
tests.hint: Replace the TODO with a real implementation.

explanation: The teardown function is the part with a cost attached. When a user navigates away and the component unsubscribes, aborting the fetch closes the connection, which is what surfaces as `RequestAborted` on the server and stops generation. Without it, the server happily finishes a two-thousand-token response that nobody will ever see, and bills for it. Handling the `error` event as a stream error rather than ignoring it is the other half: after a 200 the server has no way to signal failure except through the protocol, so the client has to be listening for it.

title: Embedding Cache with Stampede Protection
problemMarkdown:
## Problem

Implement an embedding cache that survives concurrent access.

## Requirements

- Key on a hash of the normalised text **and** the model name.
- Hold a per-key lock so only one caller computes a missing embedding.
- Re-check the cache after acquiring the lock.
- Treat a cache error as a miss rather than failing the request.

## Why this matters

Omitting the model name from the key means a model upgrade silently serves incompatible vectors — retrieval quality collapses and nothing errors.
starterCode:
class EmbeddingCache:
    def __init__(self, cache, embedder, model_name: str):
        self._cache = cache
        self._embedder = embedder
        self._model_name = model_name
        self._locks = {}

    async def embed(self, text: str) -> list[float]:
        # TODO: hash the normalised text WITH the model name
        # TODO: read the cache, tolerating cache failure as a miss
        # TODO: take a per-key lock, re-check, compute, store
        raise NotImplementedError

tests.name: Includes the model name in the cache key
tests.hint: Without it, changing embedding model silently serves incompatible vectors.

tests.name: Normalises the text before hashing
tests.hint: Identical content differing only in whitespace should hit the same entry.

tests.name: Uses a content hash rather than the raw text
tests.hint: Hash the normalised text so the key is bounded in length.

tests.name: Takes a per-key lock
tests.hint: One caller computes; the rest wait and then read the populated value.

tests.name: Re-checks the cache after acquiring the lock
tests.hint: Another caller may have populated the entry while you waited.

tests.name: Tolerates cache failure
tests.hint: A cache outage should degrade to calling the provider, never fail the request.

solutionCode:
import asyncio
import hashlib
import json


class EmbeddingCache:
    def __init__(self, cache, embedder, model_name: str):
        self._cache = cache
        self._embedder = embedder
        self._model_name = model_name
        self._locks: dict[str, asyncio.Lock] = {}

    def _key(self, text: str) -> str:
        normalised = " ".join(text.strip().split())
        digest = hashlib.sha256(normalised.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
        # The model name is part of the key: vectors from different models are
        # not interchangeable, and serving the wrong ones fails silently.
        return f"emb:{self._model_name}:{digest}"

    async def embed(self, text: str) -> list[float]:
        key = self._key(text)

        cached = await self._try_get(key)
        if cached is not None:
            return cached

        lock = self._locks.setdefault(key, asyncio.Lock())
        async with lock:
            # Another caller may have populated it while we waited.
            cached = await self._try_get(key)
            if cached is not None:
                return cached

            vector = await self._embedder.embed(text)

            try:
                await self._cache.set(key, json.dumps(vector), ttl_seconds=86_400)
            except Exception:
                pass  # a cache write failure must not fail the request

            return vector

    async def _try_get(self, key: str):
        try:
            raw = await self._cache.get(key)
            return json.loads(raw) if raw else None
        except Exception:
            return None  # cache unavailable: treat as a miss and carry on
explanation: The model name in the key is the detail that prevents a genuinely nasty failure. Vectors from different embedding models are not comparable, so if you upgrade the model and the cache keeps returning old vectors, similarity search degrades in a way that produces no error at all — answers simply get worse and nobody can explain why. Swallowing cache errors is the other deliberate choice: a cache is an optimisation, and an optimisation that can fail the request is a liability. The double-check after acquiring the lock avoids the common bug where every waiting caller recomputes anyway.

title: Managed Identity Configuration with Key Vault
problemMarkdown:
## Problem

Configure an ASP.NET Core application so that no secret appears in configuration.

## Requirements

- Use `DefaultAzureCredential` with the user-assigned identity's client ID.
- Load configuration from Key Vault using that credential.
- Register Azure OpenAI and Azure AI Search clients with the same credential.
- No connection string or API key anywhere in `appsettings.json`.

## Why this matters

`DefaultAzureCredential` resolves to the managed identity in Azure and to developer credentials locally, so the same code path works in both with no secret in either.

tests.name: Uses DefaultAzureCredential
tests.hint: It resolves to managed identity in Azure and developer credentials locally.

tests.name: Binds the user-assigned identity client ID
tests.hint: A user-assigned identity must be identified explicitly.

tests.name: Loads configuration from Key Vault
tests.hint: Key Vault becomes a configuration provider, reached via the credential.

tests.name: Registers the Azure OpenAI client with the credential
tests.hint: Pass the credential rather than an API key.

tests.name: No API keys in the code
tests.hint: Any key-based credential defeats the purpose of this exercise.

explanation: The configuration contains endpoints and a client ID — neither is a secret, and both can sit in source control. The user-assigned identity is specified explicitly because a compute resource can carry several identities and the SDK cannot guess which one you mean. Key Vault is still needed, but only for genuine third-party secrets, and reaching it through the managed identity removes the bootstrap problem entirely: there is no first secret needed to fetch the other secrets. Locally, `DefaultAzureCredential` falls back to the developer's own credentials, so the code path never diverges between environments.

title: Least-Privilege IAM Policy for an AI Task
problemMarkdown:
## Problem

Write an IAM policy for an ECS task that invokes Bedrock and reads tenant-scoped objects from S3.

## Requirements

- Allow Bedrock invocation for **named model ARNs only**, not `bedrock:*`.
- Allow S3 reads scoped to the task's tenant using a principal tag.
- Add an explicit deny for S3 access from outside the VPC endpoint.
- No wildcard resources on the allow statements.

## Why this matters

`Resource: "*"` almost always means nobody worked out what was actually needed. Naming model ARNs is also a cost control: a new expensive model cannot be invoked without a policy change.

tests.name: Allows only the named Bedrock actions
tests.hint: List the specific actions; a wildcard grants future actions you have not reviewed.

tests.name: Scopes Bedrock to specific model ARNs
tests.hint: Name the approved model ARNs so a new expensive model needs a policy change.

tests.name: Uses a principal tag for tenant scoping
tests.hint: ${aws:PrincipalTag/tenantId} gives per-tenant isolation from a single policy.

tests.name: Includes an explicit deny
tests.hint: An explicit deny wins over any allow, including ones added later.

tests.name: Conditions the deny on the VPC endpoint
tests.hint: Deny unless the request arrives through your VPC endpoint.

explanation: Three things earn their place here. Naming model ARNs rather than using `bedrock:*` is both a security and a cost control — when a new, more expensive model is released, invoking it requires a deliberate policy change rather than happening by accident. The principal tag gives per-tenant isolation from one policy instead of four hundred, and the tag is set on the role at assumption time so application code cannot alter it. The explicit deny is the belt-and-braces layer: it wins over every allow, including allows someone adds later without thinking about the network boundary.

title: Production Dockerfile for a .NET AI Service
problemMarkdown:
## Problem

Write a production Dockerfile for an ASP.NET Core AI orchestrator.

## Requirements

- Multi-stage build so the SDK does not ship to production.
- Restore dependencies in a separate layer so code changes do not invalidate the package cache.
- Run as a non-root user.
- Include a health check.
- No secrets baked into the image.

## Why this matters

A single-stage build ships a compiler and your source code to production. Running as root means a container escape starts with privileges.
starterCode:
# TODO: build stage on the SDK image

# TODO: publish

# TODO: runtime stage on the ASP.NET image, non-root, with a health check

tests.name: Uses a multi-stage build
tests.hint: A build stage on the SDK image and a runtime stage on the ASP.NET image.

tests.name: Restores dependencies in a separate layer
tests.hint: Copy the csproj and restore before copying the rest of the source.

tests.name: Runs on the runtime image, not the SDK
tests.hint: The final FROM must be the ASP.NET runtime image.

tests.name: Runs as a non-root user
tests.hint: Add a USER instruction before the entrypoint.

tests.name: Declares a health check
tests.hint: Point it at your /health endpoint.

tests.name: No secrets in the image
tests.hint: Secrets come from managed identity or the orchestrator at runtime, never from the image.

solutionCode:
# ---- build ----
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:8.0 AS build
WORKDIR /src

# Restore in its own layer: a source change does not invalidate the package
# cache, which is the difference between a 20-second and a 4-minute build.
COPY ["FutureTech.Api/FutureTech.Api.csproj", "FutureTech.Api/"]
COPY ["FutureTech.Infrastructure/FutureTech.Infrastructure.csproj", "FutureTech.Infrastructure/"]
COPY ["FutureTech.Application/FutureTech.Application.csproj", "FutureTech.Application/"]
COPY ["FutureTech.Domain/FutureTech.Domain.csproj", "FutureTech.Domain/"]
RUN dotnet restore "FutureTech.Api/FutureTech.Api.csproj"

COPY . .
RUN dotnet publish "FutureTech.Api/FutureTech.Api.csproj" \
    -c Release -o /app/publish --no-restore

# ---- runtime ----
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:8.0 AS runtime
WORKDIR /app

# Non-root: a container escape should not start with privileges.
RUN adduser --system --uid 1001 --group appuser
COPY --from=build --chown=appuser:appuser /app/publish .
USER appuser

EXPOSE 8080
ENV ASPNETCORE_URLS=http://+:8080

HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=10s --retries=3 \
  CMD wget --no-verbose --tries=1 --spider http://localhost:8080/health || exit 1

ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "FutureTech.Api.dll"]
explanation: Copying the project files and restoring before copying the source is the layer-caching trick that matters most in practice — without it every source change re-downloads every package. The multi-stage split keeps the SDK, the source and the build tooling out of the shipped image, which reduces both size and attack surface. The health check is what lets the orchestrator distinguish "starting" from "broken", and `--start-period` stops it killing a container that is still warming up. Secrets are conspicuously absent: they arrive at runtime from managed identity or the orchestrator, never baked into a layer where they persist in the image history.

title: Deployment Manifest with Probes and Limits
problemMarkdown:
## Problem

Write a Kubernetes Deployment for an AI orchestrator.

## Requirements

- Separate readiness and liveness probes — they answer different questions.
- Resource requests and limits.
- A non-root security context.
- Configuration from a ConfigMap; no secrets in the manifest.
- A `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` long enough for in-flight streaming responses to finish.

A liveness probe that checks dependencies will restart your pod during a downstream outage, turning a degraded service into a crash loop.

tests.hint: securityContext with runAsNonRoot: true.

tests.name: Allows time for in-flight streams to finish
tests.hint: Streaming responses can run for tens of seconds; the default 30s may cut them off.

tests.name: No secrets in the manifest
tests.hint: Reference a Secret or use workload identity; never inline a key.

solutionCode:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: ai-orchestrator
  labels: { app: ai-orchestrator }
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: ai-orchestrator }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: ai-orchestrator }
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: ai-orchestrator   # workload identity, not a key
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 1001
        fsGroup: 1001
      # Streaming responses can run for tens of seconds. Cutting them off at
      # the 30s default produces truncated answers during every rollout.
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 90
      containers:
        - name: orchestrator
          image: acr.azurecr.io/ai-orchestrator:1.4.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef: { name: ai-orchestrator-config }
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "500m", memory: "1Gi" }
            limits:   { cpu: "2000m", memory: "2Gi" }
          # Readiness: should we send traffic? Checks dependencies.
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /health/ready, port: 8080 }
            initialDelaySeconds: 10
            periodSeconds: 10
            failureThreshold: 3
          # Liveness: is the process wedged? Must NOT check dependencies, or a
          # downstream outage becomes a cluster-wide crash loop.
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /health/live, port: 8080 }
            initialDelaySeconds: 30
            periodSeconds: 20
            failureThreshold: 3
          securityContext:
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] }
explanation: The probe distinction is the point of this exercise and it is routinely got wrong. Readiness asks "should traffic come here?" and should check dependencies — if the search index is unreachable, take the pod out of rotation. Liveness asks "is this process wedged?" and must not check dependencies, because if it does, a downstream outage restarts every pod simultaneously and converts a degraded service into a crash loop that cannot recover even after the dependency returns. The grace period is the AI-specific detail: a streaming response can legitimately run for forty seconds, and the 30-second default truncates users mid-answer on every deployment.

title: Azure OpenAI with Private Endpoint
problemMarkdown:
## Problem

Provision an Azure OpenAI account reachable only over a private endpoint.

## Requirements

- Disable public network access on the account.
- Create a private endpoint in a private subnet.
- Wire up the private DNS zone so the endpoint resolves internally.
- Grant a user-assigned identity the data-plane role rather than using keys.

## Why this matters

A private endpoint without the DNS zone resolves to the public IP and silently keeps using the internet path — the configuration looks correct and is not.
starterCode:
resource "azurerm_cognitive_account" "openai" {
  name                = "aoai-prod"
  location            = var.location
  resource_group_name = var.resource_group_name
  kind                = "OpenAI"
  sku_name            = "S0"

  # TODO: disable public network access
}

# TODO: private endpoint
# TODO: private DNS zone and link
# TODO: role assignment for the user-assigned identity

tests.name: Disables public network access
tests.hint: Set it to false so the account is reachable only privately.

tests.name: Creates a private endpoint
tests.hint: The endpoint lives in a private subnet and targets the account.

tests.name: Configures the private DNS zone
tests.hint: Without the zone the hostname resolves to the public IP and the endpoint is bypassed.

tests.name: Links the DNS zone to the VNet
tests.hint: The zone must be linked to the VNet for resolution to work.

tests.name: Grants a role rather than using keys
tests.hint: Cognitive Services OpenAI User on the identity — no key needed.

tests.name: No keys in the configuration
tests.hint: Referencing the account key defeats the purpose.

explanation: The private DNS zone is the part that is easy to omit and impossible to notice. Create the private endpoint without it and everything appears correct — the endpoint exists, the NIC has an address — but the account hostname still resolves to its public IP, so traffic keeps taking the internet path and your compliance evidence is wrong. The `custom_subdomain_name` is a second quiet prerequisite: private endpoints on Cognitive Services accounts require it, and omitting it produces a confusing failure. The role assignment removes keys from the picture entirely, which is what makes the whole configuration auditable.
